title: The Single Point of Failure
author: Susan J. Montgomery
summary: A venture diligence professional turns her signature analytical habit — finding the single point of failure in a company — back on her own household after her husband's death, and uses the resulting personal essay to make a business argument about risk concentration. She lays out how single points of failure form invisibly and by accident: an irreplaceable technical cofounder, a customer worth 40% of revenue, an investor's name standing in for diligence nobody actually ran. Drawing on Angel Capital Association data, she argues portfolios under ten positions systematically underperform more diversified ones, framing this not as stock-picking skill but as structural resilience. The essay's turn is that she applies the same diagnosis to her marriage — her husband ran parts of their life she never learned to run, not from incapacity but from lack of necessity — and that dependency stayed invisible exactly like an undocumented codebase, until it wasn't. She closes with concrete, unglamorous fixes: document knowledge so more than one person holds it, diversify revenue and reliance, and always read the data room yourself rather than trusting someone else's name on the deal.
points: Single points of failure are rarely deliberate — they form by accident, through rewarding what's working today and never asking what happens if the one load-bearing person or customer doesn't show up tomorrow.

Angel Capital Association data shows portfolios under ten positions return well under invested capital, while portfolios of twelve-plus held five-plus years perform meaningfully better — evidence that diversification, not conviction or stock-picking talent, drives outcomes.

Angel investors often can't see their own concentration risk because it "wears the costume of conviction rather than neglect" — a hot streak on three deals gets mistaken for a strategy rather than a small sample doing what small samples do.

The fix for concentration risk is deliberately unglamorous: write down knowledge so more than one person can find it, spread revenue across more than one door that could close, and personally read the data room instead of trusting someone else's name on the term sheet.

The author's central admission — having built a career calling out this flaw in other people's businesses while never once applying it to her own household — is the piece's real argument: expertise doesn't protect you from your own blind spots.
quotes: The habit is finding the single point of failure. Every company I diligence has one. Sometimes the founder knows it and is hoping I won't ask and sometimes they genuinely don't see it, which is worse, honestly, because you can't fix what you can't name.

Nobody sets out to build a single point of failure. It gets built by accident, by rewarding what's working today and never asking the boring question of what happens if the one load-bearing thing doesn't show up tomorrow.

Broadly: portfolios under ten positions tend to return well under invested capital, and portfolios of twelve or more, held over five years plus, do meaningfully better and more reliably. That gap isn't stock-picking talent. It's whether you built something with more than one leg under it.

I built a household on one leg and didn't notice, for the same reason the undocumented codebase works fine until the one person who understands it takes a week off. My husband ran things I never learned to run.

If your company depends on the knowledge in one person's head, or one customer's renewal decision, or one investor's name standing in for diligence you never ran yourself, that isn't traction or conviction either but a single point of failure with a nicer outfit on.
The companies I got a reputation for reading correctly were never the ones hiding something from me. I was the one hiding it. From myself, mostly.
